Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.\n\nUse active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: \"Save changes,\" not \"Submit.\" An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says \"Publish\" produces a toast that says \"Published.\" The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.\n\nTreat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. \nL233:   * Troubleshoot\nL234: \nL235:   * 【21†Troubleshoot with SSH】\nL236: \nL237: [Button: Send feedback ]\nL238: # Using WebSockets Stay organized with collections Save and categorize content based on your preferences.\nL239: \nL240: This page provides guidance and best practices for running WebSockets or other streaming services on Cloud Run and writing clients for such services.\nL241: WebSockets applications are supported on Cloud Run with no additional configuration required. However, WebSockets streams are HTTP requests, which are still subject to the 【22†request timeout】 configured for your Cloud Run service, so you need to do the following:\nL242:   * Increase the 【22†request timeout】 period to the maximum duration you would like to keep the WebSockets stream open, for example 60 minutes.\nL243:   * Ensure your clients are able to 【23†reconnect】.\nL244:   * Consider using 【24†session affinity】 for clients to reconnect as much as possible to the same instance.\nL245:   * Don't enable 【25†HTTP/2 end-to-end】.\nL246: Though 【24†session affinity】 on Cloud Run provides best effort affinity, new WebSockets requests could still potentially connect to different instances, due to built-in load balancing. To solve this problem, you need to 【26†synchronize data between instances】.\nL247: \nL248: Note that WebSockets on Cloud Run are also supported if you are using 【27†Cloud Load Balancing】.\nL249: ## Deploying a sample WebSockets service\nL250: \nL251: Use Cloud Shell to quickly deploy a sample whiteboard service that uses WebSockets with Cloud Run: 【28†Deploy a sample†deploy.cloud.run】\nL252: \nL253: Or, if you want to deploy that sample whiteboard service manually:\nL254: \nL255:   1. Clone the Socket.IO repository locally using git command-line tool:\nL256: \nL257:     `git clone https://github.com/socketio/socket.io.git\nL258:     `\nL259: \nL260:   2. Navigate into the sample directory:\nL261: \nL262:     `cd socket.io/examples/whiteboard/\nL263:     `\nL264:   3. Deploy a new Cloud Run service by building the service from source code using 【29†the Google Cloud CLI】:\nL265: \nL266:     `gcloud run deploy whiteboard --allow-unauthenticated --source=.\nL267:     `\nL268: \nL269:   4. After the service is deployed, open two separate browser tabs and navigate to the service URL. Anything you draw in one tab should propagate to the other tab (and vice versa) since the clients are connected to the same instance over WebSockets.\nL270: ## WebSockets chat sample full tutorial\nL271: \nL272: If you want a full code walkthrough, additional code samples are available in the topic 【30†Building a WebSocket Chat service for Cloud Run tutorial】.\nL273: \nL274: ## Best Practices\nL275: \nL276: The most difficult part of creating WebSockets services on Cloud Run is synchronizing data between multiple Cloud Run instances. This is difficult because of the autoscaling and stateless nature of instances, and because of the limits for 【31†concurrency】 and 【22†request timeouts】.\nL277: ### Handling request timeouts and client reconnects\nL278: \nL279: WebSockets requests are treated as long-running HTTP requests in Cloud Run. They are subject to 【22†request timeouts】 (currently up to 【32†60 minutes】 and defaults to 5 minutes) even if your application server does not enforce any timeouts.\nL280: \nL281: Accordingly, if the client keeps the connection open longer than the required timeout configured for the Cloud Run service, the client will be disconnected when the request times out.\nL282: Therefore, WebSockets clients connecting to Cloud Run should handle reconnecting to the server if the request times out or the server disconnects. You can achieve this in browser-based clients by using libraries such as 【33†reconnecting-websocket†github.com】 or by handling \"disconnect\" events if you are using the 【34†SocketIO†socket.io】 library.\nL283: ### Billing incurred when using WebSockets\nL284: \nL285: A Cloud Run instance that has any open WebSocket connection is considered active, so CPU is allocated and the service is 【35†billed†cloud.google.com】 as instance-based billing.\nL286: ### Maximizing concurrency\nL287: \nL288: WebSockets services are typically designed to handle many connections simultaneously. Since Cloud Run supports 【31†concurrent connections】 (up to 【32†1,000 per container】), Google recommends that you increase the maximum concurrency setting for your container to a higher value than the default if your service is able to handle the load with given resources.\nL289: ### About sticky sessions (session affinity)\nL290: \nL291: Because WebSockets connections are stateful, the client will stay connected to the same container on Cloud Run throughout the lifespan of the connection. This naturally offers a session stickiness within the context of a single WebSocket connection.\nL292: For multiple and subsequent WebSockets connections, you can configure your Cloud Run service to use 【24†session affinity】, but this provides a best effort affinity, so WebSockets requests could still potentially end up at different instances. Clients connecting to your Cloud Run service might end up being serviced by different instances that do not coordinate or share data.\nL293: To mitigate this, you need to use an external data storage to synchronize state between Cloud Run instances, which is explained in the next section.\nL294: ### Synchronizing data between instances\nL295: \nL296: You need to synchronize data to make sure clients connecting to a Cloud Run service receive the same data from the WebSockets connection.\nL297: \nL298: For example, suppose you are building a chatroom service using WebSockets and set your 【31†maximum concurrency】 setting to `1,000`. If more than `1,000` users connect to this service at the same time, they will be served by different instances, and therefore, they will not be able to see the same messages in the chatroom.\nL299: To synchronize data between your Cloud Run instances, such as receiving the messages posted to a chatroom from on all instances, you need an external data storage system, such as a database or a message queue.\nL300: If you use an external database such as 【36†Cloud SQL†cloud.google.com】, you can send messages to the database and poll from the database periodically. However, note that Cloud Run instances 【37†do not have CPU】 when the container is not handling any requests. If your service primarily handles WebSockets requests, then the container will have CPU allocated as long as there is at least one client connected to it.\nL301: Message queues work better to synchronize data between Cloud Run containers in real-time, because the external message queues cannot address each instance to \"push\" data. Your services need to \"pull\" new messages from the message queue by establishing a connection to the message queue.\nL302: Google recommends that you use external message queue systems such as 【38†Redis Pub/Sub†redis.io】 (【39†Memorystore†cloud.google.com】) or 【40†Firestore real-time updates】 that can deliver updates to all instances over connections initiated by the container instance.\nL303: #### Using Redis Pub/Sub\nL304: \nL305: 【41†Image: WebSockets chatroom service architecture】\nL306: \nL307: You can use the 【38†Redis Pub/Sub mechanism†redis.io】 by creating a Redis instance from 【39†Memorystore†cloud.google.com】. If you are using the Socket.IO library for WebSockets, you can use its 【42†redis adapter†github.com】.\nL308: In this Redis-based architecture, each Cloud Run instance establishes a long-running connection to the Redis channel that contains the received messages (using the 【43†`SUBSCRIBE`†redis.io】 command). Once the container instances receive a new message on the channel, they can send it to their clients over WebSockets in real-time.\nL309: Similarly, when a client emits a message using WebSockets, the instance that receives the message publishes the message to the Redis channel (using the 【44†`PUBLISH`†redis.io】 command), and other instances that are subscribed to this channel will receive this message.\nL310: \nL311: If you want a full code walkthrough, additional code samples are available in the topic 【30†Building a WebSocket Chat service for Cloud Run tutorial】.\nL312: \nL313: [Button: Send feedback ]\nL314: Except as otherwise noted, the content of this page is licensed under the 【45†Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License†creativecommons.org】, and code samples are licensed under the 【46†Apache 2.0 License†www.apache.org】. Starting another flow in the same browser replaces the cookie; complete one connection at a time.\n\nAES-GCM uses a fresh 96-bit IV and authenticated client/role/account context. Altered ciphertext and cross-role token substitution fail decryption. `oauth.accessToken(role)` validates before every use and refreshes only after validation 401, or an explicit retry after a Helix 401. New refresh tokens are encrypted and saved only after validation. A shared-store 30-second lease serializes refresh/save operations and rejects expired writers; contention fails with a retryable busy error rather than running parallel refreshes. The default HTTP transport has an eight-second per-request timeout, rejects redirects, and redacts transport errors. Network failures after Twitch rotates a token but before storage commits can require reconnecting the account; there is no distributed transaction with Twitch.\n\n## Bot and EventSub\n\n`createRuntime(env, { transport, firestoreClient })` returns the HTTP handler plus OAuth/bot/store services. Dependencies are injected in tests. `runtime.bot.sendChat(message)` is an internal trusted service method; it sends to the configured streamer with the configured bot's validated user token and sender ID. It limits messages to 500 Unicode code points, retries a 401 once after refresh, and treats dropped messages/errors as failures. It does not automatically reply to events. This user-token path can send to all channels in a Twitch Shared Chat session; a source-only app-token sending path is not implemented.\n\n`runtime.bot.chatSubscription()` builds the webhook `channel.chat.message` version 1 payload. `runtime.bot.subscribeChat()` validates both prior grants, obtains an app token using client credentials and submits that payload. These methods make live requests only when called; neither startup nor tests invoke live services. No public control endpoint, automatic subscription provisioning, reconciliation, or raid-subscription registration is included. Do not call them against Twitch until separately authorized.\n\n`POST /eventsub` verifies HMAC-SHA256 over ID + original timestamp + exact raw bytes with a timing-safe digest comparison before parsing. It caps bodies at 64 KiB and rejects malformed JSON/UTF-8, invalid signatures, stale (>10 minutes), future timestamps and invalid consumed schemas. Verified challenges return HTTP 200 raw text with Content-Length equal to the UTF-8 byte length. HTTP 204 acknowledgements omit body, Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding. Duplicates do not repeat mutations.\n\nRaid notifications create a **local 90-second ritual starting at verified receipt processing**, never synchronized with Twitch. Chat notifications require the configured streamer/bot subscription condition and matching host/event schema. Ordinary chat atomically stores only the latest bounded receipt metadata per host (message/chatter IDs and receipt time), not raw chat text. Recognized marks commands instead use the private marks engine below; mark submissions retain only their normalized text privately for moderation. A signed chat event alone is not proof that a chatter arrived in the raid. There is still no claim endpoint: future claims must require participation from **both incoming raiders and host chat**, with membership/proof rules still to be designed. Revocations are acknowledged/deduplicated; subscription lifecycle and grant deletion are pending.\n\n## Must milestone: marks backend and original runes\n\nThe marks milestone added the backend engine/store integration. The next overlay increment adds a read-only public snapshot and WebSocket below; there are still no public mark mutation, moderation or pending-text endpoints. All service methods are internal trusted interfaces; do not expose them to request-supplied actor objects.\n\n**Fail-closed context:** `app.marks.setKeeperContext(hostId, { streamId, keeperId, optedIn, holdsRelic, blockedUserIds })` requires an explicit authoritative session ID, numeric Keeper ID, boolean consent/ownership, and a bounded configured blocked-user list. Acceptance requires that the Keeper ID equals the signed chat broadcaster, consent is true and the Keeper holds the relic. Only a trusted lifecycle/ownership integration may call this method. Tests inject synthetic trusted contexts; live stream lifecycle and ownership/opt-in synchronization are **not wired yet**. Runtime startup supplies no context, so real marks remain disabled. No ID is inferred from dates, raid events, names or viewer text. Updating the same active stream ID preserves viewer quotas. Selecting a new authoritative stream closes the previous session and removes its viewer quota identifiers; closed stream IDs cannot be reactivated to obtain fresh budgets. Cooldowns survive that transition until their original 30-second expiry.\n\n`!mark word` or `!mark emoji` submits a mark through the already authenticated `channel.chat.message` boundary. Inputs receive Unicode NFKC, locale-independent lowercase and explicit sharp-S/final-sigma folding. The bounded conservative policy accepts one letters/combining-marks word or one supported emoji grapheme (including ZWJ families, modifiers, flags and keycaps). It rejects spaces, control/bidi/invisible word characters, HTML/link syntax and a small substring blocklist. Input is capped at 128 UTF-8 bytes and 32 normalized code points. The filter is intentionally conservative, can reject benign text, and is not comprehensive multilingual abuse/confusable moderation; moderator approval is still required.\n"
      }
    }
  ]
}

This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.\n\n## Ground your designs in the subject matter\n\nIf the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.\n\n## Design principles\n\nFor web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.\n\nTypography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.\n\nChoose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\n\nDefault to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.\n\nAvoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:\n- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.\n- Using all caps for labels.\n- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.\n\nVisual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.\n\nUse non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.\n\nConsider written content carefully. This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.\n\n## Restraint and self-critique\n\nSpend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.\n\n## Design principles\n\nFor web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.\n\nTypography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.\n\nChoose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\n\nDefault to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.\n\nAvoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:\n- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.\n- Using all caps for labels.\n- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.\n\nVisual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.\n\nUse non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.\n\nConsider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.\n\n## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique\n\nFor calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:\n1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);\n2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;\n3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;\n4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;\n5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.\n\nAll traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.\n\nWork in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.\n- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.\n- Type: the typefaces and their roles.\n- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?\n- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.\n\nThen review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.\n\nWhen writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.\n\n## Restraint and self-critique\n\nSpend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.\n\n## More on writing in design\n\nWords appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.\n\nWrite from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.\n\nUse active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: \"Save changes,\" not \"Submit.\" An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says \"Publish\" produces a toast that says \"Published.\" The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.\n\nTreat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened.         "output": "# Raid Relic\n\nAn original, evolving relic travels between Twitch communities: a verified raid brings it to the next room, and two chats bind it together. Each completed hand-off adds a gold growth ring and carries approved community runes into a recorded journey. The transparent OBS artwork, Atlas constellation and replay make that shared history visible—without treating chat presence as proof of raid membership.\n\n## Judge in 60 seconds\n\n1. Open the **[P9 browser demo](https://p9-stretch---raid-relic-vz4bhnskgq-uc.a.run.app/demo/)**. No Twitch login, installation or credentials are needed. Press **Autoplay 35-second tour**.\n2. Pause to take over, or Reset → Send Off → offer early → simulate receipt → accept. Tab/Enter operate the controls; reduced motion uses static presentation. Download a zero-ring **SIMULATED DEMO** PNG if you like.\n3. Open the **[P9 Atlas](https://p9-stretch---raid-relic-vz4bhnskgq-uc.a.run.app/atlas/)** for recorded stops, configured Keepers, badges, local replay and per-stop ring cards. Reading never opts a viewer into public scores.\n\nThe permanently labelled demo starts with fictional Keepers and zero rings. It runs only in browser memory: **no API, socket, provider or storage writes** (`connect-src 'none'`). The Atlas is separate and reads retained public records.\n"

No embeds, avatar trackers or remote artwork are added.\\n\\n`/keeper/raidrelichq` and `/keeper/olsols2` show retained received rings, approved community glyphs from the latest received stop, real from/to names and UTC completion dates. Reads do not create score consent or membership.\\n\\nEach recorded ring can be downloaded as an original-art **1200×675 (16:9)** or **720×1280 (9:16)** PNG, bounded to 512 KiB. A recorded card does not imply the destination still holds the relic.\\n\\nCompleted stops expose **Twitch-reported raid audience**, taken from the signed raid receipt's existing retained `raidSize`. All provider traffic is injected/mock; no physical evidence is claimed. (IAM, infrastructure as code, containers/Kubernetes, service mesh, serverless/edge, ingress, provider events, or runtime configuration): use [CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md](CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md).\n>\n> caches/search, object links, analytics, export/backup, migration, deletion, retention, or restore): use [DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md](DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md).\n>\n> **Desktop, mobile, and local-IPC targets** (native apps, deep links, webview bridges, exported components, privileged helpers, local daemons, Unix sockets/XPC/Binder/D-Bus): use [DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md](DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md).\n\n**Injection** (subagent_type: `general`)\nTrace untrusted input from entry point to dangerous sink. What counts as a \"dangerous sink\" depends on the application:\n- Web apps: SQL queries, HTML output, shell commands, template engines, file paths, HTTP redirects, deserialization\n- Libraries: any function that processes caller-supplied data without validation — buffer operations, parsers, format strings\n- CLI tools: shell command construction, file path handling, environment variable interpolation\n- Services: query construction, message serialization, log injection, LDAP/XPATH queries\n- Client-side (browser/JS): DOM XSS, prototype pollution, `postMessage`/origin trust, and other browser-side classes — covered by the [CLIENT-SIDE.md](CLIENT-SIDE.md) companion blocks when selected\n\nDo not stop at the obvious direct paths. Look for indirect injection: data stored safely, then retrieved and used in a dangerous context by different code. Look for injection through field names, keys, headers, and metadata — not just values. Look for injection into secondary systems (logs, caches, search indexes, analytics).\n\n**Access control** (subagent_type: `general`)\nVerify that a caller cannot do something outside its authority. Go beyond checking whether permission checks exist — verify they check the *right* permission for the *right* resource via the *right* mechanism:\n- Is there a path to the same state change that checks a different (weaker) permission?\n- Can a field in the request body override what the permission system intended to restrict?\n- Are there endpoints that gate on authentication but forget authorization?\n- Does the same resource have multiple access paths with inconsistent checks?\n- What about bulk/batch/export/import operations — do they enforce per-item permissions?\n\nFor complex access models, split into separate agents for auth bypass vs authorization logic.\n\n**Resource and file handling** (subagent_type: `general`)\n- Path traversal (reading/writing outside intended directories) — including through symlinks, encoded sequences, and null bytes\n- SSRF (making the application fetch attacker-controlled URLs) — including through redirects, DNS rebinding, and URL parser differentials\n- Unsafe deserialization, archive extraction (zip slip), temp file handling\n- Memory safety (if applicable): buffer overflows, use-after-free, integer overflow\n- Race conditions on file operations (TOCTOU between check and use)\n\n**Cryptography and secrets** (subagent_type: `general`)\n- Weak randomness for security-critical values (tokens, keys, nonces)\n- Hardcoded secrets, secrets in logs, error messages, URLs, or client-visible responses\n- Broken key derivation, missing HMAC verification, nonce reuse\n- Timing side-channels on secret comparison\n- Misuse of crypto primitives (ECB mode, unauthenticated encryption, static IVs, etc.)\n- What happens when crypto operations fail? Does the error path fall back to no-crypto?\n\n**Business logic** (subagent_type: `general`)\nHunt logic errors by hand: standard scanners cannot find them, and they yield high-impact findings. For each major workflow:\n- **State machine violations**: Can you skip steps? Go backwards? Reach an invalid state? What happens if you replay a completed flow? What about partial failure — if step 2 of 3 fails, is step 1 rolled back?\n- **Race conditions with business impact**: Concurrent operations that produce invalid states (double-spend, double-approve, lost updates). Focus on operations that check-then-act non-atomically.\n- **Numeric/quantity manipulation**: Negative values, zero values, overflow, precision loss, type coercion between string and number.\n- **Access boundary violations**: Not \"does the permission check exist\" but \"is it the right check for the business rule?\" Can input to one operation bypass a restriction enforced on a different operation for the same effect?\n- **Implicit trust assumptions**: Data from storage, config, other components, or plugins assumed safe because \"we validated it on the way in.\" What if a different code path wrote it?\n- **Time-based logic**: Expiry checks, scheduling, rate windows, clock skew. What happens at exact boundary moments? What about timezone differences between components?\n- **Default and fallback behavior**: What is the security posture when config is missing? When a feature flag is off? When a dependency is unavailable? When the system is mid-migration?\n\n**Feature abuse and data leakage** (subagent_type: `general`)\nLegitimate features used for unintended purposes. Look for bugs in the design, not only in the code:\n- **Export/backup as exfiltration**: Can a low-privilege user trigger an export, snapshot, or backup that includes data above their access level? Can they export other users' data? Does the export include deleted/draft/private content? Revision history that was supposed to be pruned?\n- **Import/restore as injection**: Can import overwrite existing data? Can it create records that bypass normal validation? Can it inject content into collections the user has no write access to? Does it respect the same permission model as the UI?\n- **Search/filter/sort as oracle**: Can search queries reveal whether content exists that the user cannot directly access? Do filter parameters let users probe statuses, roles, or fields they should not know about? Does sorting by a hidden field reveal its values through result ordering?\n- **Enumeration through side effects**: Do error messages differ between \"does not exist\" and \"no access\"? Do response times differ? Response sizes? HTTP status codes? Can you enumerate users through password reset, invite, or registration flows?\n- **Preview/draft/staging leakage**: Are preview tokens scoped to one item or do they unlock broader access? Can draft content be discovered through search, RSS feeds, sitemaps, or API listing endpoints? Can cache headers cause a CDN to serve private content publicly?\n- **Notification/webhook as SSRF**: Can a user set a notification URL, webhook URL, or callback URL that the server fetches? Is it validated against internal networks? What about after a redirect?\n\n**Chained vulnerabilities and trust boundaries** (subagent_type: `general`)\nIndividually allowed or contained behavior can become a vulnerability when another component or lifecycle step relies on a stronger guarantee:\n- **Multi-step boundary failures**: Map what a low-privilege principal may read, write, invoke, and retain, then connect only concrete outputs to later trust decisions. Confirm each prerequisite and do not assume a downstream effect.\n- **Cross-component trust gaps**: Component A validates input and passes it to component B. Compare the exact guarantee A produces with what B assumes, including truncation, type coercion, normalization, tenant scope, and plugin/extension access.\n- **Second-order use**: Data safe when stored may become dangerous in a later context. A field name becomes a JSON path, a slug becomes a file path, escaped text enters raw rendering, or a stored string becomes a URL, regex, template, or policy expression.\n- **Scope and capability growth**: Token, API-key, plugin, OAuth, MCP, or AI capabilities become broader after delegation, refresh, caching, role change, or composition. Name the concrete operation the resulting principal should not have.\n- **Timing and ordering**: Review setup, migration, soft-delete, revoke/cache expiry, check/use, and validate/consume windows. Confirm stale state is accepted before reporting.\n- **Rollback and recovery**: Undelete, restore, revision rollback, and cancellation must apply current ownership, validation, and authorization. Confirm which invalid state is restored.\n\n**Wildcard** (subagent_type: `general`)\nYou are not given a category. Find vulnerabilities outside the standard classes already assigned.\n\nRead code that looks boring or disconnected from security. Follow incomplete, experimental, compatibility, and fallback features, but retain the same concrete boundary and validation requirements as every other class.\n\nUse these starting points, but do not limit yourself to them:\n- What is the strangest code in the codebase? Why does it exist? What happens if it is abused?\n- Are there any features that feel half-finished, experimental, or bolted on? Those have the weakest security because they got the least review.\n- What happens if you use the API in a way the frontend never would? The UI constrains users, but the API does not. What API calls are possible but never made by the client?\n- Are there any hidden or undocumented endpoints, parameters, headers, or features? Look at route registrations, middleware, and config for things that are not in the docs.\n- What happens when you mix features that were not designed to work together? Localization + preview + caching. Import + plugins + webhooks. OAuth + impersonation + API keys.\n- Is there anything interesting in the git history? Reverted security fixes, commented-out auth checks, secrets that were committed then removed (still in history).\n- Which valid-account actions affect other users, shared integrity, availability, or operator-owned cost? Verify containment, quotas, authorization, and recovery around those actions.\n- Which operations are irreversible or require elevated confirmation? Bind authorization and approval to the final principal, action, and resource.\n- What assumptions does the code make about the environment? That the database is local, that the clock is accurate, that DNS is trustworthy, that the filesystem is case-sensitive?\n- Look at the test files — what are they **not** testing? Compare the edge cases the developer thought about (tests exist) with the ones they did not (no tests).\n\nPursue anomalies inside your assigned scope until the invariant is settled. If something looks strange, read it until you can state whether it is safe. If a function has a comment explaining why it is safe, verify the explanation. If a variable is named `temp` or `hack` or `legacy`, read it closely.\n\n**Obvious things** (subagent_type: `general`)\nOther agents hunt subtle bugs. This agent checks the basic exposures that are easy to overlook because everyone assumes someone else already checked them:\n- Are there any hardcoded passwords, API keys, tokens, or secrets in the source? (grep for `password`, `secret`, `apikey`, `token`, `Bearer`, `-----BEGIN`, common default passwords)\n- Are there any TODO/FIXME/HACK/XXX comments that reference security? (`TODO: add auth`, `FIXME: validate input`, `HACK: skip permission check`)\n- Is debug mode / dev mode properly gated? Can it be enabled in production via environment variable, query parameter, or header?\n- Are there test/example/seed credentials that work in production?\n- Is there a `/debug`, `/admin`, `/test`, `/status`, `/health`, `/metrics`, `/env`, `/.env`, `/config` endpoint that is unprotected?\n- Are there any `.env`, `.env.local`, `credentials.json`, `*.pem`, `*.key` files checked into the repo?\n- Does the `.gitignore` actually cover secrets, uploads, and local config?\n- Are dependencies pinned? Are there known CVEs in the dependency tree? (check lockfiles)\n- Are there any `eval()`, `exec()`, `child_process`, `Function()`, `vm.runInContext`, `import()` with dynamic input?\n- Are CORS headers set to `*` or overly permissive? Is `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` combined with a wildcard origin?\n- Are cookies missing `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, or `SameSite` attributes?\n- Are there any open redirects? (parameters named `redirect`, `return`, `next`, `url`, `goto`, `continue` that feed into redirects without validation)\n- Is TLS enforced? Are there any HTTP-only endpoints?\n- Are error responses in production returning stack traces, internal paths, or SQL errors?\n\nThis agent does not need to be creative. It needs to be thorough and literal. Check every item. Report each result.\n\n**Important**: For any finding this agent reports, it must verify the full code path, not just surface appearance. If a cookie is missing `HttpOnly`, check whether the cookie contains security-sensitive data and whether JS needs to read it by design. If an error message contains a field name, check whether the field is ever actually populated with sensitive data. A flag is not a finding — trace the impact before reporting.\n\nEXACT GUIDANCE WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md\n# HTTP-Protocol and Authentication Hunting\n\n#### When to use this file\n\nReach for this file when the target speaks HTTP at a parsing, caching, browser-authentication, or identity boundary: web applications, APIs, reverse proxies, CDNs, gateways, custom HTTP servers, and services implementing sessions, JWT, OAuth/OIDC, SAML, password recovery, MFA, passkeys, API keys, or mTLS. Use this with `ATTACK-CLASSES.md`: access-control review asks whether a principal may perform an operation; this file asks whether the HTTP or identity layer can confuse which principal, request, assurance level, or token the operation belongs to.\n\nPick classes from Phase 1. Split a large target into request framing and cache policy, browser authentication, federated identity, strong authentication and recovery, service credentials, and session lifecycle. A single server behind an unobserved managed proxy has little source-confirmable smuggling surface; a proxy or custom parser has much more.\n\n## Core discipline (include in every agent prompt for this domain)\n\n```\n- Framing and cache findings require two interpretations of the same request, response, or key. A valid webhook signature authenticates a provider delivery; chat location does not prove that someone actually joined a Twitch raid. Provider acceptance of a bot message does not prove that viewers saw it.\\n\\n## Review and evidence\\n\\nThe October 27 source review was a quick, scoped review of nine assigned boundaries, not a complete penetration test. Parent-operated offline Node 22 fixtures reproduced all 15 baseline scenarios after fixture corrections (source225, 4.805 seconds, zero skips). Those scenarios exercised post-authentication dummy interfaces and reducers; they did not measure actual Twitch throughput. The hardening changes and expanded regression tests require fresh operator execution before publication. See the dated [quality record](QUALITY.md) and the exact publication CI for accepted cohorts; historical regression totals are not blanket security clearance.\\n\\nThe changes keep the existing 128 receipt/outbox and 256 presence bounds. Score receipts have per-actor and per-room admission limits; command ACKs and sharing receipts have per-actor limits. Excess requests do not allocate another receipt. Completion reservations can replace non-completion bookkeeping, but preserve existing completion receipts, including unknown delivery outcomes. Full sharing storage declines admission without throwing or altering an existing alias. Outer message-proof deduplication prevents duplicate sharing work; retained minimal hashed receipts protect accepted and rate-rejected requests through alias changes.\\n\\nPresence is optional proof for a moved-source participant. Saturation declines additional proof without evicting existing participants or aborting independent direct commands. Full revocation storage advances a conservative global `notBefore` watermark and invalidates older presence. This lets forgetting commit while delayed old messages remain unable to restore forgotten proof. Quotas and cooldowns are not refunded.\\n\\n## Write-path matrix\\n\\n| Path | Input and identity boundary | Limits, state and output controls | Source and regression references |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n| Send Off | Signed broadcaster command or exact own authenticated control; configured target | Current holder, consent, policy, matching live streams and fresh grant/moderator checks; persisted dispatch boundary before provider POST; ambiguous outcomes are not automatically retried | `src/send-state.js`, `src/send-off.js`; `test/send-off.test.js`, `test/reliability-demo.test.js` |\\n| Claim | Signed verified raid plus distinct original chat participants on the correct sides | Transactional quorum, receipt clock, current streams/policies, deduplication and bounded lineage; no transfer from mere HTTP acceptance | `src/claims.js`, `src/store.js`, `src/state.js`; `test/claims.test.js`, `test/security-hardening.test.js` |\\n| Seeker | Own broadcaster identity or own CSRF-protected control | Timestamp barrier, explicit opt-in, current-holder exclusion and receipt dequeue; former holder must explicitly rejoin; status does not change membership | `src/lifecycle.js`, `src/seeker-state.js`; `test/seeker-state.test.js` |\\n| Marks and moderation | Original signed actor; broadcaster/moderator checks for privileged actions | Normalized bounded word/emoji, five marks per viewer per stream and cooldown; held text private; forget/block/veto purge retained derived copies | `src/marks.js`, `src/claims.js`; `test/my-marks.test.js`, `test/security-hardening.test.js` |\\n| Chat replies | Configured room and bound actor, not caller-selected provider identity | Actor/room budgets, bounded receipts and queues; closed failures; completion and request deduplication | `src/bot.js`, `src/scoreboard.js`, `src/claim-ack.js`; `test/recording-replies.test.js` |\\n| OAuth callback | Exact callback path, expiring browser-bound one-time state, configured role | Validate provider client, principal and required scopes; random-IV AES-GCM encrypted role-bound token pairs; per-role singleflight, distributed refresh lease and atomic save | `src/oauth.js`, `src/crypto.js`; `test/oauth.test.js` |\\n| Controls and sibling actions | Exact own account/session, Origin and CSRF; bounded strict request bodies | Read-only master gate precedes mutations; session rotation/CAS; cancellation and recovery bind exact generation; request body cannot choose another principal | `src/control.js`, `src/pilot.js`; `test/pilot.test.js`, `test/onboarding.test.js` |\\n\\n## Public rendering, exports and privacy\\n\\nPublic projections expose only approved retained engravings. Runes are generated from original numeric geometry; stored words do not become arbitrary SVG markup. Browser text uses text nodes/textContent and canvas fillText, not untrusted HTML. Public exports omit private mark-owner identifiers, held words and raw chat. Card generation rechecks the public stop, approved marks, journey and current holder before saving; races cancel export. Forgetting removes retained application associations and derived copies while preserving minimal existing quota/cooldown accounting. Already saved local PNGs cannot be recalled. See [sharing](SHARE_CARDS.md) and [membership policy](SEEKER_MEMBERSHIP.md).\\n\\nOAuth scopes remain role-specific. Optional bot permissions do not silently become requirements for base grants. Access-token expiry can trigger validated before-use renewal under the existing lease; only definitive refresh rejection requires renewed consent, while transient provider failures remain temporary. Irreversible Raid POSTs are not replayed on 401. Cached control status does not acquire a fresh grant merely to display readiness.\\n\\nA Twitch client ID is a public identifier, not a bearer credential. Parent previously classified seven historical scan findings as that public identifier, with zero unresolved findings at that checkpoint; this is not a claim about all future repository contents. The operator reruns release hygiene scans. Tokens, authorization codes, state cookies, raw provider bodies and private transcript entries must not be copied into reports. Raid diagnostics bound and redact sensitive input; other warnings use closed enums and structured severity. Public errors must not expose raw exceptions. Evidence is selected and sanitized; raw credential-bearing logs are not committed.\\n\\n## Remaining boundaries and external gates\\n\\nDurable OAuth-state expiry and cleanup require a dedicated resource-lifecycle review and owner verification of actual Firestore retention policy. No TTL job or paid service was added. The disabled internal Wander write path was not independently covered by this initial hunting wave; existing tests exercise purpose HMAC, nonce and generation/CAS controls, but are not a substitute for that review. Wander remains off and its owned cron remains commented pending explicit owner GO.\\n\\nDependency/native-binary vulnerabilities, cloud IAM, proxy behavior, hosted retention and provider configuration were not independently audited here. Repository history hygiene belongs to the operator's sanitized scan process. Physical Twitch/OBS delivery and consent remain owner-observed gates. Synthetic fixtures, a zero-traffic preview and source inspection do not establish those physical results or authorize promotion. No scopes, pilot admission, schedulers, resources or paid features change in this increment.\\nEOF\",\"max_output_tokens\":1000}));\n"
